idiom_name: single superclass plus protocol conformances with default implementations in protocol extensions
implementation_notes: Swift supports one superclass and deliberately has no multiple inheritance: the language diagnostics reference states that multiple inheritance 'is unsupported in Swift. Instead, Swift allows composition of interfaces using protocols'. So the second hierarchy becomes protocol conformances - a type may conform to any number of protocols, protocol composition (A & B) states the combined requirement, and a protocol extension supplies overridable default implementations. What replaces the twin link: both capabilities exist on one object, and where the classic pair is still justified (a second parent that must own stored state, since protocol extensions cannot add stored properties) the usual Swift answer is a collaborator or delegate reference rather than a second half of the same entity, with the back-reference marked weak to avoid a retain cycle.
pitfalls: Protocol extensions cannot add stored properties, so a 'parent' that carries state cannot be replaced by a protocol - the fallback is the classic two-object pair or an explicit collaborator.
A method declared only in a protocol extension (not in the protocol) is statically dispatched: whether your implementation runs depends on the static type, and the class's own method may be ignored.
A default implementation that a conforming base class does not override cannot be overridden in its subclasses (a documented limitation of protocol defaults combined with class inheritance).
A class-held collaborator that points back at the class keeps both alive unless one reference is declared weak or unowned; Swift will not infer this for you.
